concepts.objective: Identify changes in the population, measurement or target-generating process and distinguish within-environment performance from evidence about deployment.
Distinguish prediction from intervention targets and explain why neither predictive strength nor a causal label alone guarantees robustness.
Compare conditional relationships across environments and state the mechanism and support assumptions needed for a scoped invariance argument, without treating stability as causal proof.
Design external-environment checks for prediction and generation, including content preservation, failure monitoring and abstention when evidence does not cover the intended use.

sources.citation: Peters, Jonas; Janzing, Dominik; Schölkopf, Bernhard. Elements of Causal Inference: Foundations and Learning Algorithms. MIT Press, 2017.

claims.proposition: A relationship useful for prediction in observed environments need not apply in a new environment whose generating processes or support differ.

source_refs.locator: Section 8.3, Domain Adaptation, environments and equation (8.7)

claims.proposition: The most informative observational predictor need not be an effective intervention target, because prediction and changing the target are different tasks.

source_refs.locator: Section 6.3, Example 6.10, Predictors and intervention targets

claims.proposition: Under a causal model, changes to other mechanisms can leave the target mechanism invariant. Domain generalization additionally assumes that the relevant conditional relationship persists in the test environment and has adequate support; stability can also occur for non-parent predictor sets.

source_refs.locator: Section 6.6, equation (6.7); Section 8.3, equation (8.7), discussion of non-parent sets and overlapping supports

claims.proposition: Evidence from multiple environments is interpreted under assumptions about which mechanisms change. Hidden variables and previously unexamined mechanism changes can invalidate an invariance argument.

source_refs.locator: Section 8.3, equation (8.7) assumptions; Section 9.5.6, restrictions on hidden variables and environment interventions

claims.proposition: Reference counts and assessment cases in this pack are authored teaching data. Interactive experiment outcomes are deterministically recomputed from the released model and learner settings. Ratios, differences and weighted sums use declared denominators and target weights. Generation fidelity and withholding criteria are declared teaching-model rules, not empirical guarantees or textbook claims about a particular generator.

resources.text: A warehouse assistant predicts parcel damage from recorded image features and drafts an inspection report. Another warehouse has different packaging and lighting. The old test score does not cover those conditions.
Worked example

List the cases, how measurements are taken and what the checking label means. A new warehouse can change several of these at once. A different mix of cases is not the same change as a less reliable measurement or a different process producing the outcome.

For a prediction, compare with a suitable reference label: a separate label used for checking. The teaching model sets its reference label before adding measurement error; it is not a real clinical or inspection review. Real use requires suitable checking information. Matching a report to its recorded source does not establish independent truth.

Evaluate on records from the intended warehouse that were not used to fit or tune the system. Keep the checking-label definition appropriate. A fresh random split from the old site answers an old-site question; it does not recreate changed measurements or a new mix of cases.

Prediction estimates an outcome or label from available data; generation produces text from a source. Distribution shift is a change in the kinds of cases, their measurements, or the relationship being predicted.
A lower score shows a performance gap, not which change caused it. An old-site score is not a guarantee for a new site.
Name the new conditions, then check both predictions and reports under those conditions.
Testing the intended setting provides evidence about that use. The records must be separate from training and tuning, and their checking labels must suit the task.
That check can miss errors introduced by the new setting. Consider which measurements and cases were actually tested.
Ask which records contain the conditions the assistant will actually face.
An assistant was tested only on records from one warehouse. Another warehouse uses different measurements and has a different mix of cases. Which check directly tests the proposed new use?
Testing the intended setting provides evidence about that use. The records must be separate from training and tuning, and their checking labels must suit the task.
Stable writing quality does not check source fidelity or independent factual correctness. Changed inputs require content checks in the intended setting.
A fluent report can still omit or change a fact. Check what the proposed test actually measures.
Writing quality and factual preservation are different properties of a report.
After a camera change, a description generator keeps the same writing-quality score. Nobody checks whether its descriptions still match the photographed items and records. What is still needed?
Stable writing quality does not check source fidelity or independent factual correctness. Changed inputs require content checks in the intended setting.
A warehouse label appears more often on damaged parcels. Editing only that label in a recorded input can change a prediction without changing the parcel's condition.
Worked example

Predicting the reference label asks what information the warehouse label provides. An intervention actively changes a variable. Editing the recorded marker changes an input to the assistant, but the exercise keeps the underlying condition and its reference label fixed. A prediction change is not a change in that condition.

The warehouse label can be associated with the kinds of cases sent to each warehouse. That pattern may help in one dataset and fail when the case mix or marking convention changes. An association with a checking label is not evidence that changing the marker would improve the underlying outcome.

A plausible causal explanation can help choose a feature, but the predictor receives its measured value. The experiment's content rule reads a noisy target measurement, not a feature established to cause the target. Poor measurement, a new range of cases or a changed outcome-producing process can invalidate prediction. Removing one shortcut does not validate all remaining inputs.

A cue is a clue used for prediction. A spurious cue can predict well here without causing the outcome. A causal feature is proposed to affect the outcome; it is not a reliability guarantee. Poor measurement or a changed outcome process can still break prediction.
Do not confuse changing a model's prediction with changing the outcome. A causal label also does not repair a bad measurement.
Ask separately what helps predict, what would change the outcome and what has actually been tested.
The edit tests dependence on a recorded input. The exercise holds the underlying condition fixed; it does not test a treatment for changing that condition or guarantee other predictions.
A model output and the condition it describes are not the same thing. Look at what the edit actually changed.
Separate the input, the predicted label and the underlying condition.
An assistant uses a warehouse label to predict a recorded outcome. In this exercise, editing only that marker leaves the underlying condition unchanged. What does a changed prediction show?
The edit tests dependence on a recorded input. The exercise holds the underlying condition fixed; it does not test a treatment for changing that condition or guarantee other predictions.
A causal explanation may motivate an input, but its measurement still matters. Relevant case ranges and the outcome-producing process also need checking.
A causal claim and a measurement claim are separate. Consider what information the predictor actually receives.
The predictor receives a measured value, not direct access to the proposed cause.
Suppose a material property affects parcel damage in a proposed causal model. A new camera measures that property poorly. Does including it guarantee reliable predictions there?
A causal explanation may motivate an input, but its measurement still matters. Relevant case ranges and the outcome-producing process also need checking.
Two warehouses report 85% overall accuracy, but the second makes more errors on fragile parcels. The same overall score can hide a change within that group.
Worked example

A conditional comparison compares outcomes or errors for cases with the same relevant measured features. An overall average mixes those cases together. Differences in group sizes can hide different group errors. Check the relevant groups, enough observations and a consistent checking-label definition rather than relying on equal overall scores.

A mechanism is the process producing an outcome from its causes. A stability argument may assume this process stays the same while site labels or the case mix change. It also needs suitable measurements. If the new setting changes the outcome-producing process itself, the old argument does not automatically apply.

Support means the feature values and kinds of cases represented in the data. Comparing overlapping ranges avoids pretending that unseen cases were tested. Stable patterns can also occur without a direct causal link, so observations from a few sites do not uniquely identify a causal graph or cover an untested range.

An invariant relationship stays the same across the settings compared. Using it elsewhere needs assumptions about the outcome-producing process, measurements and the kinds of cases covered. Stability alone does not prove a cause or guarantee future performance.
Equal averages can hide different errors. Even a stable within-group relationship is evidence under assumptions, not proof of a unique causal graph.
Say which relationship stayed stable, which changes were tested and which new conditions remain untested.
The comparison supports stability over the tested ranges. It does not prove a cause, validate unfamiliar feature ranges or establish that a new outcome process is unchanged.
The comparison covered particular settings and ranges. Check whether the proposed conclusion reaches beyond them.
Useful evidence can have a limited scope without proving every causal or future claim.
Across three warehouses, cases with the same relevant measured features have similar outcome patterns over overlapping feature ranges. Which conclusion is justified?
The comparison supports stability over the tested ranges. It does not prove a cause, validate unfamiliar feature ranges or establish that a new outcome process is unchanged.
Overall accuracy mixes groups. Compare relevant within-group behaviour over comparable ranges, with enough data to judge uncertainty; a matching average alone does not do this.
A single average mixes different kinds of cases. Examine the reported group difference rather than setting it aside.
Ask whether the same average could hide different errors in the groups that matter.

Two warehouses both report 85% overall accuracy. One makes more errors on fragile parcels at the second warehouse, where group sizes differ. Does the equal average establish stability for similar parcels?
Overall accuracy mixes groups. Compare relevant within-group behaviour over comparable ranges, with enough data to judge uncertainty; a matching average alone does not do this.
A fluent draft changes 'no crack found' to 'crack present'. A second draft copies a mistaken source correctly. The first fails source fidelity; the second still needs an independent factual check.
Worked example

For prediction, define the label being predicted and compare predictions with appropriate independent reference labels. For generation, specify the source facts that must be retained, the additions that lack source support and important omissions. Clear wording is useful, but a style score does not check these factual requirements.

Report the number of source-supported reports among all cases as well as among issued reports. Withholding difficult cases can improve the latter fraction while fewer people receive a full report. If no reports are issued, fidelity among issued reports is not defined, rather than automatically perfect.

Abstention means withholding a prediction or report under a stated rule and referring it for review. Define the trigger and who reviews it. Check the intended setting, relevant groups and unfamiliar measurement ranges, then monitor errors and re-evaluate when conditions change. A withheld claim is not a verified answer, and none of these checks promises zero errors.

Report fidelity means keeping recorded source facts without inventing details. It is not proof that the source is true. Prediction accuracy compares with separate reference labels. Coverage is the share receiving a full report; withholding a report leaves that case for review.
A faithful copy can preserve a measurement error. A withheld report lowers coverage; it does not make an unsupported case correct.
Check reference accuracy, source fidelity and the fraction receiving reports, with a clear review rule for gaps.
The draft reverses the recorded source assertion. Checking source fidelity is separate from checking fluency and from establishing whether the source itself is correct.
Improved wording does not settle whether the report retained the source's meaning. Read the two factual statements again.
Compare the meaning of the two statements, not just their style.
A draft changes 'no crack found' in its source to 'crack present'. Its writing-quality score improves. Which assessment is justified?
The draft reverses the recorded source assertion. Checking source fidelity is separate from checking fluency and from establishing whether the source itself is correct.
A review rule makes the missing information and untested setting visible. Withholding a claim is not a verified answer; new evidence is needed before widening use.
The proposed rule must address the missing evidence. Confidence or an old score cannot supply the absent source fact.
Ask whether the required fact is actually available and whether this setup was evaluated.

A review rule makes the missing information and untested setting visible. Withholding a claim is not a verified answer; new evidence is needed before widening use.
